title: Oscar and the Smile
premise: Edmund Joubert, a meticulous pest controller, is called to the Holloway farm where something in the walls leaves fingerprints too large to be human and too gentle to be hostile. Her habit of documenting everything becomes a lifeline when her overnight sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud—a voice that knows her name, her dead sister's name, and the exact number of days until the old well refills. As the count dwindles, Edmund realizes the Holloways are not the thing's victims but its wardens, bound by a generational duty to keep it fed and hidden. To survive, she must break that covenant: get the family out before the well refills, knowing the thing will follow whoever carries its memory—and that documentation, once a prayer, has become an invitation.
about_author: J. M. Winterbourne is the pen name of a former rural building inspector who spent eleven years crawling through other people's basements and never stopped taking notes. They write horror about people who believe paperwork can hold back the dark.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. A routine job at the Holloway farm turns strange: droppings that aren't droppings, grease smears at shoulder height of something very tall. Edmund photographs everything out of professional habit. Emotional beat: unease disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. In the pantry she finds prints pressed into flour—human-shaped but eight inches long, five fingers, no calluses. The Holloway patriarch, Aldous, watches her photograph them and says nothing. She logs the date. Beat: the first crack in her professional detachment.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Edmund, with flashback texture to her sister's death and the notebooks she kept afterward. We learn why she records: if she writes it down, it stays outside her. She sets up a recorder for the night shift. Beat: ritual as armor.

chapters.title: What the Walls Want
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She traces movement through wall cavities, finds a nest of chewed documents—old Holloway letters, decades of them, softened into pulp. Something here reads. Or used to read. Beat: dread deepening into curiosity.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Reviewing the night recording, she hears herself talking in her sleep—and a second voice, low and patient, answering questions she never asked. It says her sister's name. She plays it eleven times. Beat: terror fused with longing.

chapters.title: Aldous Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She confronts Aldous; he offers coffee, deflection, and one sentence: 'It only counts what you give it.' His wife Mara flinches at the word counts. Their teenage son Wren stares at Edmund's notebook like it's a wound. Beat: the family's complicity surfaces.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Well House
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She breaks into the locked well house and finds a ledger: names, dates, offerings, going back to 1911. Every Holloway birth is entered. So is a column labeled DAYS TO REFILL. The current page is nearly full. Beat: the shape of the trap becomes visible.

chapters.title: Wren Knows More Than He Says
chapters.summary: POV alternating Edmund/Wren. Wren admits he talks to it at night—it asked him once what the ocean was like, and he lied. He's terrified of the day it stops believing him. Edmund recognizes her own rituals in his. Beat: alliance forming across generations of silence.

chapters.title: Counting Down
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The ledger's refill date is nine days out. Fingerprints now appear on her car windows, on her notebook cover, arranged almost tenderly. The recordings grow longer each night; the voice asks better questions than most living people do. Beat: seduction inside horror.

chapters.title: Mara's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Edmund/Mara. Mara reveals the covenant: the thing was given the family in 1911 in exchange for the farm's survival through a famine winter. Leaving means it follows the memory-bearer. Mara stayed so her children wouldn't have to go. Beat: love against duty, stated plainly.

chapters.title: Nine Questions
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The voice asks her nine questions over three nights—about grief, about whether being remembered is the same as being loved. She answers honestly on tape and hates how much lighter she feels after. Beat: the horror begins to feel like intimacy.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Left
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She tracks down a Holloway cousin who fled in 1987: a hollowed man in a care facility who still writes the same ledger entry every day, though the well is two hundred miles away. It followed him. It's still following him. Beat: the cost of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Plan for Extraction
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She drafts the plan: all four Holloways leave together, split the memory deliberately—each carrying a fragment so no single person holds the whole. Documentation becomes strategy instead of prayer. Aldous refuses; the land is his duty. Beat: resolve hardening against resistance.

chapters.title: Aldous Goes Down to the Well
chapters.summary: POV Edmund/Aldous. Aldous descends to negotiate an extension, speaking into the dark the way his father did. What answers uses his dead father's voice. He comes up having bought six days and lost something he won't name. Beat: duty revealed as slow self-destruction.

chapters.title: The Night It Touched Me
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. Half-asleep, she feels fingers—gentle, enormous—resting on her sternum like it's checking she's real. The recorder captures forty minutes of near-silence and one sentence: 'You document because no one documented you.' Beat: the armor cracks open.

chapters.title: Three Days to Refill
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The well begins to sound wet. Wren runs; Edmund retrieves him from the tree line where the fingerprints have circled him like parentheses. She promises him the ocean—the true answer to the thing's question. Beat: protective love crystallizes into commitment.

chapters.title: Betrayal by Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She discovers a new entry in the ledger in handwriting identical to hers: her own name, dated tomorrow. The thing has been reading her notebooks all along. Documentation was never a prayer—it was a signature. Beat: devastating reversal of her core belief.

chapters.title: Burning the Archive
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. She burns her notebooks and the ledger in the yard, keeping only one page hidden against her skin. The house screams through its walls. Aldous finally agrees to leave—not for himself, but because he sees what the archive did to her. Beat: sacrifice of identity.

chapters.title: Out Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The family flees at dawn in two vehicles, splitting the memory fragments between them per the plan. The thing stands at the property line—seen fully for the first time, tall and patient and grieving—and does not cross. It counts them out loud as they pass. Beat: escape laced with unbearable pity.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: POV Edmund, from a motel two states away. Water sounds fill the night recording anyway. The hidden page is warm. One by one, the family members report dreams of a voice asking gentler questions. The covenant isn't broken; it's renegotiated. Beat: false relief, rising dread.

chapters.title: What Follows Memory
chapters.summary: POV Edmund. The cousin in the care facility dies peacefully the same hour the well refilled—released. Edmund understands: it doesn't hunt, it collects what it's owed, and it has decided she is worth keeping. She chooses to stop running and start answering. Beat: acceptance as agency.

chapters.title: Oscar and the Smile
chapters.summary: POV Edmund, epilogue. She learns its name from the 1911 letters: Oscar, a son given to the well. She visits the farm alone, sits at the wellhead, and smiles—for the first time answering rather than recording. The count ends not with escape but with witness. Beat: bittersweet resolution; love against duty, resolved by choosing both.
